title: A tingle at station 12
note: Fictional unit. Test methods and limits come from the recurrent-test standard and the service manual; outlets and circuits are the facility electrician’s work.
intro: You are the biomedical technician. At 14:20 on Tuesday the charge nurse calls you to station 12. Mr. Ben Aquino, dialyzing through a fistula, says he felt a tingle when his free hand touched the metal side panel of machine 12. The floor under the station had just been mopped. The machine is running normally with no alarms.

choices.text: Keep everyone’s hands off the case, and ask the nurse to get him off machine 12 by the physician’s decision.
choices.feedback: A tingle means current is flowing from the case through a person to earth. The case may not be earthed, or there is leakage, or both. Moving or ending his treatment is a clinical decision; your part is to make sure the machine comes out of use.
choices.then: The physician has the session ended and his blood returned. Machine 12 is unplugged and tagged out of service.

choices.text: Connect your analyzer and measure the leakage now, while it runs.
choices.feedback: Testing comes after the patient is safely off. A machine suspected of leaking current is not tested with a patient connected to it.
choices.then: The charge nurse stops you. The physician has the session ended; machine 12 is unplugged and tagged out of service.

choices.text: The wet floor explains it: dry the floor, give him a dry towel to rest his hand on, and let the session finish.
choices.feedback: A wet floor makes it easier for current to flow through a person, but a properly earthed machine with normal leakage should not give a tingle. The fault is still there when the floor dries.
choices.then: The charge nurse calls the physician, who has the session ended. Machine 12 is unplugged and tagged out.

choices.text: Visual inspection: plug, cord, strain relief, case, signs of fluid.
choices.feedback: Many electrical faults can be seen before a meter is connected. Inspect in the same order every time, and fix what you find before testing.
choices.then: The cord jacket is crushed and split near the plug, where a machine wheel has run over it. There are water marks on the cabinet base.

choices.text: Go straight to the leakage current test on the analyzer’s automatic sequence, since that measures the actual hazard.
choices.feedback: The analyzer comes after the eyes. A split cord or water inside the case is a fault already, and finding it first can save time and an analyzer.
choices.then: Before connecting, you notice the cord: crushed and split near the plug. There are water marks on the cabinet base.

choices.text: Open the cabinet and look for loose wires inside.
choices.feedback: Inside may matter, but the outside comes first: plug, cord, strain relief, case. The commonest faults are visible there.
choices.then: Before opening it, you see the cord is crushed and split near the plug, and there are water marks on the cabinet base.

n3.scene: With the cord lying still, protective earth resistance reads 0.25 Ω. The limit for a detachable cord is 0.3 Ω. When you flex the cord near the split, the reading jumps to open circuit.

choices.text: Fail. Replace the cord with the approved part, dry and check the cabinet, then repeat the full test.
choices.feedback: A broken strand that touches in one position and parts in another is why you flex the cord during the earth test. An earth that opens when the machine is moved is no earth.
choices.then: With the new cord, the earth holds at 0.08 Ω while flexed. You dry the cabinet, find a leaking drain connector, and fix it. Leakage current is now within the limit.

choices.feedback: The reading that counts is the worst one. A nurse moving the machine flexes the cord the same way you just did.
choices.then: You reconsider and replace the cord. The earth holds at 0.08 Ω while flexed; you dry the cabinet and fix a leaking drain connector.

choices.text: Wrap the split with electrical tape so the strands stay in place, and test it again.
choices.feedback: Never tape a cord. Replace it with the approved part.
choices.then: The chief technician has you replace the cord. The earth holds at 0.08 Ω while flexed; you dry the cabinet and fix a leaking drain connector.

n4.scene: You check the station 12 wall outlet with your outlet tester. It shows an open earth. The next patient for station 12 is booked tomorrow at 06:30.

choices.text: Station out of use; the electrician repairs it; test every other station outlet.
choices.feedback: A perfect machine on an ungrounded outlet is not protected. The outlet is the facility electrician’s to repair and verify. If one has failed, check the rest and update the outlet list with the dates.
choices.then: The electrician finds a loose earth connection and repairs it that evening. Two other outlets also test faulty and are repaired.

choices.text: Run tomorrow’s machine from station 13’s outlet through an extension lead.
choices.feedback: Extension leads and multi-socket adapters are not used for dialysis machines. They add resistance to the earth path and may have no earth at all.
choices.then: The charge nurse refuses. You ask the electrician, who repairs the outlet that evening and finds two other faulty outlets.

choices.text: Report the outlet to the electrician, and keep station 12 out of use until he has repaired and verified it.
choices.feedback: Right for station 12. But a station that failed for months unnoticed raises the question for every other outlet: test them too.
choices.then: The electrician repairs it that evening. When you test the others, two more are faulty and are repaired.

n5.prompt: What do you do before machine 12 returns?

choices.text: Record and release by procedure, report the event, and route cords off the floor.
choices.feedback: Record each value against its limit, the analyzer used, the faults found and fixed, and your name. Report the event, check the other machines’ cords for the same crush damage, and keep cords out of the wheels’ path and away from wet floors.

choices.text: Release it with a note saying “cord replaced.”
choices.feedback: That hides the earth failure, the water leak, the outlet, and the patient’s report. The record and the event report are how the unit learns.

choices.text: Release it, and ask the cleaners not to mop the floor while machines are running, since the wet floor started the whole thing.
choices.feedback: The wet floor revealed the fault; it did not cause it. Record the full repair, report the event, and stop cords being run over.

end.title: The next week
end.text: Two other machines have cords with early crush marks; both are replaced before they fail. Cord hooks are fitted at every station. The outlet list now shows a verified date for each station, and the event report has gone to the quality meeting.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A tingle is current through a person. Get the patient off the machine by clinical decision, and take it out of use.
  • Inspect before you test. Many faults are visible.
  • Flex the cord during the earth test; the worst reading counts.
  • The outlet is part of the protection. Never use extension leads; check every station when one fails.
  • Record and report everything you found.
